When you call something highfalutin, you are saying it is trying too hard to seem grand, impressive, or important — but in a way that feels fake, overdone, or unnecessary. It is the word you reach for when something (or someone) is puffed up with a sense of its own importance.

Think of it this way: imagine a person who uses ten complicated words when one simple word would do just fine, who speaks in a grand, theatrical voice even in casual conversation, and who acts as though everything they say deserves to be carved in stone. That person — or their speech, or their attitude — is highfalutin.
The Three Main Things It Describes

Highfalutin is most commonly used to describe three things: language, behavior, and ideas.

1. Highfalutin language is language that is unnecessarily fancy, flowery, or complicated. It uses big, impressive-sounding words or overly elaborate sentences where plain, simple language would communicate the same thing far more clearly. The speaker or writer seems to be more interested in sounding sophisticated than in actually saying something useful. A politician who uses long, ornate sentences stuffed with jargon to say something that could be said in ten plain words is using highfalutin language.

2. Highfalutin behavior refers to acting in a way that is snobbish, self-important, or superior — as if the person is above ordinary people or ordinary things. It is the attitude of someone who puts on airs, meaning they perform a level of refinement or importance that is exaggerated or unearned. A neighbor who refuses to attend community events because they consider them "beneath" them has a highfalutin attitude.

3. Highfalutin ideas or plans are ones that are grandiose — far more ambitious or lofty in their presentation than they deserve to be, or wildly impractical in their scope. When someone frames a very ordinary goal in enormous, sweeping, dramatic terms — as though they are about to change the fate of civilization — their plans sound highfalutin.

This is important: highfalutin is not a neutral word. When you use it, you are almost always mocking or criticizing what you are describing, even if gently. You are rolling your eyes. You are saying, in effect: "Come on. Drop the act. This is not as impressive as it's being made to sound."

The word itself has a folksy, down-to-earth flavor. There is something almost deliberately unpretentious about it — which is exactly why it works so well to puncture pretension. A plain-spoken farmer calling a city lawyer's speech "highfalutin" captures the attitude perfectly.

This means the word often carries a slight sense of humor — a gentle, knowing smirk. It is not usually an angry insult. It is more of a wry, grounded observation that something is overdressed and overblown.
The Spectrum: Mild vs. Strong Use

The word can be used across a range of intensities.

On the milder end, you might use it affectionately or playfully — "you don't need all those highfalutin words with me" said to a friend who just showed off their vocabulary. Here, it's teasing.

On the stronger end, it can be a real criticism — "the company's mission statement is full of highfalutin language that means nothing" — suggesting that the fancy words are actually hiding an emptiness of substance.

To sharpen the definition, it helps to draw some boundaries.

Highfalutin does not simply mean complicated. A physics textbook is complicated, but it is not highfalutin — the complexity serves a real purpose. Highfalutin means the complexity (or grandeur, or fanciness) is unwarranted — it exists for show.

Highfalutin does not simply mean formal. A formal speech at a graduation is not automatically highfalutin. But if that speech becomes so stuffed with grand, hollow phrases that it loses meaning entirely, it tips into being highfalutin.

The key element is always the gap between appearance and reality — something presenting itself as more elevated, important, or sophisticated than it truly is.

• "I just asked him what time the meeting starts, and he gave me this highfalutin speech about the nature of time management. Just answer the question!"
  • "The restaurant had a highfalutin menu — every dish had a three-paragraph description, but the food was nothing special."
  • "She has some highfalutin ideas about rebranding the entire company, but no actual plan for how to do it."
  • "He's a bit highfalutin for my taste — he corrects everyone's grammar at dinner parties."
  • "Stop using those highfalutin words. Just say what you mean."

To further anchor the meaning, here are words that share its territory: pompous, pretentious, grandiose, bombastic, snobbish, self-important, affected, ostentatious, inflated. Among these, pretentious and pompous are its closest cousins in everyday use. However, highfalutin is distinctly more informal, more colorful, and carries a more playful, folksy edge than any of those alternatives — it is the word a person with their feet firmly on the ground would use.

If you need to lock it into one sentence: Highfalutin describes something or someone that is excessively grand, fancy, or self-important in a way that feels fake, overdone, or unearned — and the word is almost always used to mock or gently deflate that pretension.
